fields.h1: Build a Mileage Reimbursement Form That Prices Every Trip
fields.hero_description: Tell Emergent your rate and your approver. It builds the mileage reimbursement form, prices each trip at the rate for its date and saves every claim as a row you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Blank Mileage Sheet Leaves Out
fields.features_subheading: A printed form leaves the rate and the math to whoever fills it in. Each piece below moves one of those jobs into the form.
fields.feature_1:
The IRS rate picked by trip date

Store each rate with the day it took effect, and every trip is priced at the rate in force when it was driven. In 2026 that matters: the business rate changed on July 1.
fields.feature_2:
Odometer readings turned into miles

Ask for start and end readings on each trip, and the form subtracts one from the other. A round-trip box doubles a one-way distance before the claim adds up the day.
fields.feature_3:
Commute miles taken off each day

Save each driver's normal drive to the office on their profile once. The form subtracts it on any day that starts at home, leaving only business driving on the claim.
fields.feature_4:
Tolls and parking on their own lines

Add tolls and parking under the mileage, each with a photo of its receipt. The app reads the amount from the photo and keeps those costs apart from the per-mile total.
fields.feature_5:
A second approver above a dollar line

Send routine claims to the driver's manager and larger ones to a second approver at a dollar amount you choose. Each decision is saved on the claim with a name and time.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take with you

Export the full codebase to your GitHub on paid plans when IT wants the mileage app on its own servers. The claims table and the history of every rate you paid come along.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Teams That Pay for Business Miles
fields.tab_content_1:
Two IRS rates on one claim

Dana Okafor drives between the buildings she manages for Cedar Row Property Group. Her claim for June 23 through July 2 crosses the mid-year rate change. June's 120 miles are priced at 72.5 cents and July's 80 at 76 cents, the rate for trips on or after July 1. Her $147.80 total needs no fixing in payroll.
fields.tab_content_2:
Six visits and no commute miles

Nurses at Willow Creek Home Care start most days at home and drive straight to patients. Leah logs six visits and odometer readings that come to 58 miles. The form takes off her usual 12-mile drive to the office, which the agency counts as commuting, and pays 46 miles at 76 cents: $34.96.
fields.tab_content_3:
School-to-school miles nobody has to guess

Pine Hollow School District shares a speech therapist between Lincoln Elementary and Oak Ridge Middle. Mei picks both schools from a route table the business office keeps, and the form fills in 4.2 miles. Her 18 October trips come to 75.6 miles, paid at the board's rate of 65 cents: $49.14.
fields.tab_content_4:
A $331.62 claim lands with the director

Larkspur Bakery's district managers visit each of their stores monthly. Sam's October claim covers 412 miles at 76 cents plus $18.50 in tolls, read from two receipt photos. Anything over $300 needs the regional director, and Rosa Delgado gets it as a direct message. Her approval syncs it to QuickBooks.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Mileage Reimbursement Form
fields.howto_description: Answer three questions before you write the prompt: which rate you pay, which miles count and who signs off.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Find the line in your policy that sets the rate per mile. Some employers pay the IRS business rate and others set their own, like a board-approved 65 cents. If the policy says nothing, agree on a rate with finance before you build.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write down the offices, job sites or schools your staff drive between. When the same routes repeat every month, record the distance for each pair once. A dropdown of known routes stops people estimating miles anyone could look up.
fields.howto_step_3_des: The IRS treats the drive between home and a regular workplace as commuting. Decide whether your policy subtracts it on days that start at home, and whether a round trip is entered once or as two separate legs.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Put the rate, the commute rule, the route list, and the approver into one plain-English prompt. Emergent builds the mileage reimbursement form, the claims table behind it, and the calculation for each trip. Ask for changes the same way later.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Pick how often people file, weekly or monthly, and how many days they have once the period closes. A deadline keeps each claim close to the driving it describes, and the app can remind anyone who has not filed yet.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Choose who signs off and where they see each request, such as a Slack message or an email. Set a dollar line for a second approver if large claims need one. Approved claims can sync to payroll or accounting software through its API.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Before rollout, submit a test claim that crosses a month end, with one round trip and one toll. Compare the form's total with your own math, then open the claims table and read the saved row field by field.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is blank PDFs and printable grids (eForms, Justia, eSign, a school district, YWCA, BoloForms, US Legal Forms) plus one Formplus blog post. Each ends in a line like 'Total miles ___ x ___ per mile', leaving the filer to type the rate and do the multiplication. In 2026 the IRS business rate changed mid-year, 72.5 cents through June 30 and 76 cents from July 1, which a single rate box cannot handle. This page says what the form must record for the IRS, answers the rate and proof questions, and shows four teams whose form prices trips by date, subtracts the commute, fills school-to-school distances and routes large claims with tolls attached. Receipts-based expense reports stay on their sibling page.

claims_to_source: The IRS business standard mileage rate for 2026 is 72.5 cents per mile for January 1 to June 30 and 76 cents per mile from July 1 to December 31
IRS car expense records include the mileage for each business use, the total miles for the year, the date, the destination and the business purpose
Records should be made at or near the time of the use, and a timely kept record carries more weight than a later statement
With incomplete records, the IRS accepts your own written or oral statement with specific detail plus other supporting evidence
If you use the standard mileage rate you cannot deduct actual car expenses such as gasoline, but business tolls and parking are deductible in addition
Driving between home and your main or regular place of work is commuting and is not deductible
